(Shira Li Bartov) 8 min. V ILNIUS, Lithuania — Archaeologists have uncovered the full floor of Lithuania’s historic Great Synagogue, revealing treasures nearly erased by Nazi and Soviet occupations — and exposing rifts between Lithuanian Jews over how to preserve and interpret what survived. Locals walking through the center of Vilnius now pass a hole in the ground, a portal to the rich Jewish past of a city once called the “Jerusalem of the North.” For the first time since 1940, they can see the polished, colorful floor and entire prayer platform of the Great Synagogue of Vilna, built in the 17th century, which became one the most important religious, cultural and intellectual hubs for Diaspora Jews. In Lithuania’s small remaining Jewish community, less than 3,000, there is no debate that the site must be preserved. But how to protect the past — and what to build over it — is a debate triggering pain over one of the last pillars of identity left standing for Lithuanian Jews. The community’s main body wants to build a new Jewish community center over the excavation, where visitors could view the Great Synagogue floor through a glass layer or a basement-level exhibit. Above, the center would mark current-day Jewish life through cultural, social and educational events. Some Jews oppose this. They say that the synagogue should be rebuilt as a house of worship or preserved as an archaeological exhibit. Other residents say the mission of a new building should be broadened beyond Lithuanian Jews, offering a center that promotes tolerance, human rights and understanding of Jewish history among all Lithuanians. 10+-year-long excavation O n the eve of WW II, the massive Great Synagogue stood among more than 100 synagogues and Jewish study houses in Vilnius, where about 40% of people were Jewish. Over 90% of Lithuanian Jews were killed in the Holocaust. From 1944 until 1990, Vilnius was remade as the capital of the Soviet Lithuanian Republic. The Great Synagogue was burned and largely destroyed by the Nazis, then razed by the Soviets to build a school in its place. “This is the place that half the population of Vilnius would have identified their city with,” Jon Seligman, the archaeologist leading the excavation, says. “So this city at the moment is missing half its identity, and because it’s such a long time since it happened, it doesn’t even know it’s missing half its identity.” The excavation is over a decade in the making. Seligman, an Israel-based archaeologist whose Jewish grandparents lived in Lithuania before WW II, first proposed unearthing the synagogue’s remains in 2013 after a visit to discover his family roots. His team of archaeologists have worked there since 2015, and last year, the former Soviet school building over the site was demolished. In an accident of history, the synagogue’s main floor was constructed below ground and spared from total erasure. “When the building was built in the 17th century, part of the restrictions that were placed on the Jewish community was that they were not allowed to build their synagogue higher than any of the churches in the surroundings,” said Seligman. “So to create the internal majesty, if you don’t want to have a low, two-story building, what you do is you drop the floor level one story below ground surface — and that’s what they did.” The latest installment of Seligman’s project, completed in July, fully exposed this main hall and the bimah , the prayer platform, covered in red, white, green and black geometric designs. Archaeologists also found traces of the Shulhoyf, a busy complex that formed the heartbeat of Jewish life. Fragments of a gefilte fish dish and a Passover plate that were found at the Great Synagogue excavation site. (Shira Li Bartov) V ilnius — Vilna in the native Yiddish nomenclature — was a major center of Jewish thought. It was home to the Vilna Gaon (1720-1797), one of the most influential Jewish sages in the last half millenium — and also the birthplace of the Jewish Labour Bund, the secular, socialist, anti-Zionist organization. Schools taught literature and the sciences in Yiddish and Hebrew. Zionist streams debated anti-Zionists and each other. Before WW II, the Shulhoyf hosted 12 prayer houses, a bathhouse, kosher butcher stalls, the first public toilets in Vilnius, the prestigious Strashun Library and the headquarters of the Yiddish Scientific Institute, or YIVO. YIVO, now in New York City, continues to preserve the Yiddish language and cultural heritage of Eastern European Jews. Faina Kukliansky, who has since 2013 chaired the umbrella organization known as the Lithuanian Jewish Community, spear- headed the initiative to construct a community center over the shul. Kukliansky grew up as the child of Holocaust survivors in Lithuania under the Soviets. She said the new space will replace the community’s current headquarters, hosted in an building that that struggles with heating and water system issues. She believes the new center will honor both the past and the present of Lithuanian Jews, featuring a YIVO exhibition alongside concerts, social clubs and Jewish learning events. After the Holocaust and decades of Soviet restrictions on Jewish life, those who remain are mostly secular and distant from Jewish traditions. Kukliansky believes that the center’s construction over the remains of the Great Synagogue will inspire Jews to trace the threads of their heritage. Conflicting visions K ukliansky’s plans have met sharp opponents from other corners of Lithuania’s Jewish world. Among the most vocal is Rabbi Sholom Ber Krinsky, an emissary for the Chabad movement who was born in Boston and has lived in Vilnius since 1994. Krinsky said that according to Jewish tradition, the Great Synagogue site should not be covered by a building for secular cultural activities, but remain a “living Jewish religious center that continues the learning and the prayer.” “If a site was used as a synagogue — for centuries, in this case — the holiness retains its holiness, and it’s proper to respect that holiness,” said Krinsky. “A Jewish community center might be nice, but it certainly doesn’t represent the holiness of that site.” Krinsky has for years asked more money for Chabad projects, which he says would be used for religious services, Jewish education and social welfare programs. He accuses Kukliansky of monopolizing funds granted to Jews by the Lithuanian government as compensation for property stolen during the Holocaust. The Good Will Foundation, an international body created through the World Jewish Restitution Organization and the Lithuanian Jewish Community, has been author- ized to distribute this restitution money. Since legislation passed by the Lithuanian parliament in 2022, the Good Will Foundation has disbursed about $9 million to compensate individual Holocaust survivors and their heirs for private property claims. Given that most Jewish property was left without heirs, another $40 million is being allocated to support Jewish communal life — including projects like the new community center. Krinsky said these funds have not been sufficiently used to nourish religious life. Kukliansky countered that her organization supports the Choral Synagogue, the only synagogue still active in Lithuania, where Krinsky leads the small group of Jews, barely a minyan for public prayers. Compared with other Eastern European communities, Chabad’s footprint is small in Vilnius, where the Vilna Gaon opposed chasidism and embodied the classical “Litvak,” which became central to the identity of almost all Lithuanian Jews. Kukliansky claims that Krinsky has refused to provide her with financial reports. K ukliansky faces further criticism from Dovid Katz, an American-born, Vilnius-based scholar of Yiddish and the Holocaust. Katz advocated for rebuilding the Great Synagogue or preserving its remnants as a religious site, which he said would draw Orthodox pilgrims from around the world. “A synagogue is a religious place, and religious leaders today — and everyday religious Jews — need to be consulted on what’s going to replace the Great Synagogue,” said Katz. “It is a place either for a replacement synagogue or for archaeological remains.” Still other critics say that Kukliansky’s community body has split the site from a broader mission that would attract non-Jewish Lithuanians and Jews from around the world. Anna Avidan, founder of Jerusalem of the North, which celebrates Jewish history in Lithuania, led a conference in 2017 that invited historians, architects and students to discuss the future of a space commemorating the Great Synagogue. Avidan said attendees proposed a cultural center that would host forums about tolerance, drawing international visitors and educating Lithuanians about the Jewish past of their country. She bellieves it would be “selfish” to build a center exclusively for the Lithuanian Jewish community, since such spaces are closed to the public, partly for security reasons. The proposals emerging from Avidan’s conference were shut down after Kukliansky’s opposition. “We are still working on how to include Jewish history in Lithuanian history,” said Avidan. “Approaching the site as a site of Lithuanian history, that would promote this harmony and understanding.” Memories of these ghosts A t the excavation site, Seligman’s team has dug up pieces of life in the synagogue, which seated about 500 people, with some 500 more squeezing in for High Holidays. The latest artifacts to emerge from the ground include a Passover plate, a dish for gefilte fish, a plaque engraved with the Ten Commandments and several seating plaques with the names of people who donated to the synagogue, assuring their seats inside. These name plaques left clues about families who vanished from Vilnius. One marked a seat for Gitel Klachek, identified as the “wife of the late Yechezkel, Shamash d’Mata” — the city sexton. Their wealthy, influential family owned several businesses around the Great Synagogue. On the uncovered synagogue floor and the surrounding Jewish neighborhoods, “there would have been a large contingent who would have been ultra-Orthodox. There also would have been a large contingent who were completely secular,” said Seligman. “The city was very, very much a very mixed community.” The fights over the memory of these ghosts — and over Lithuania’s Jewish identity — echo the disagreements that animated the Jews who once thrived there, at least after the Enlightenment began to break down traditional Jewish communities after the period of the Vilna Gaon. https://baltic-review.com/vilnius-opens-.text: Share Tweet 0 The BIO CITY III development adds new capacity for cell therapy and personalised medicine in Vilnius. VILNIUS — Lithuania has opened a €61 million centre dedicated to cell therapy and personalised medicine, adding a new advanced-technology facility to the country’s growing life-sciences sector. The centre, developed by Northway Biotech within the BIO CITY III complex at the Vilnius City Innovation Industrial Park, was officially opened on September 3. Its launch was reported by the company and by Lithuanian media, including ELTA and LRT/BNS. The project is being presented as the first dedicated facility of its kind in the Baltic states. A new stage for Vilnius’ life-sciences cluster The 3,500-square-metre building is designed for the development and manufacture of advanced biological products. According to the project information, it contains up to 20 independent production lines that can operate in accordance with current good manufacturing practice requirements. Its planned areas of work include cell therapies, personalised therapeutic vaccines and regenerative-medicine products. The centre is also intended to support the development of three-dimensional human-tissue printing technologies. These activities place the facility at the intersection of biotechnology, pharmaceutical manufacturing and applied medical research. Northway Biotech describes the building as an expansion of its existing contract-development-and-manufacturing capabilities. In practical terms, such facilities work with biotechnology and pharmaceutical partners that need specialist development, testing and manufacturing capacity for complex products. Investment combines private and public finance The total investment is €61 million. Lithuania’s national development bank ILTE provided a €48 million loan through its business-financing programme, while the remainder is being financed by Northway. The financing structure reflects the scale and technical requirements of the project. Advanced-therapy manufacturing requires specialised clean-room infrastructure, quality systems and highly trained staff. Establishing these capabilities in Vilnius may allow companies working in the field to carry out more stages of development and production within Lithuania rather than relying entirely on facilities elsewhere. National country-promotion platform Lithuania.lt said the centre is expected to employ around 100 specialists. The roles will include work in biotechnology, bioengineering, molecular biology and related life-sciences disciplines. The company has also said that initial customer programmes have already been secured, although detailed commercial information has not been made public. Part of a wider BIO CITY development The new building is one element of Northway’s broader BIO CITY development in Vilnius. The group’s existing activities include biological-drug manufacturing and a gene-therapy centre, while BIO CITY III is intended to add further capacity for advanced therapies and related services. For Vilnius, the project links industrial development with the city’s effort to attract high-value research and technology activity. The site is located in the Vilnius City Innovation Industrial Park, an area designed to accommodate companies working in research-intensive sectors. The opening also gives Lithuania a larger physical base for a field that depends on cooperation between companies, universities, laboratories and public institutions. The new centre is not a university research institute, but its work is expected to connect with the wider life-sciences ecosystem through specialist recruitment, technology development and partnerships. Why the development matters Cell and gene-based technologies are among the more technically demanding areas of modern biomedicine. Their development requires specialised production environments and strict quality controls. A local facility does not by itself guarantee that a therapy will reach patients or that every project will succeed, but it can improve the infrastructure available to companies developing such products. The centre’s opening therefore represents an industrial and research milestone rather than the announcement of a particular treatment. Its significance lies in the capacity being created: production lines, controlled facilities, specialist jobs and a platform for collaboration with international customers. Lithuania has spent recent years building a profile in lasers, biotechnology and other research-intensive industries. The BIO CITY III investment strengthens that profile by adding infrastructure for personalised medicine and cell-based technologies in the capital. Whether the centre reaches its full potential will depend on the projects it attracts, the specialists it employs and the partnerships formed around it. For now, its opening marks a concrete expansion of Lithuania’s advanced-life-sciences base and another step in Vilnius’ development as a regional biotechnology location. Luca Niculescu and Vasile Tofan / Photo: gov.ro Bogdan Matei , 28.10.2026, 14:00 Formed from a portion of the eastern Romanian territories annexed by the Stalinist Soviet Union in 1940 following an ultimatum, the current Republic of Moldova proclaimed its independence from Moscow on August 27, 1991. On that same day, Romania became the first country in the world to recognize the statehood of its new neighbor. Throughout the 35 years that have since elapsed, Bucharest has remained the most consistent and vigorous supporter of the Republic of Moldova’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and, more recently, of its European integration. It has become customary for new heads of state or government in Bucharest and Chișinău to make their first foreign visit, immediately following their inauguration, to the neighboring country. The new Romanian Prime Minister, Luca Niculescu, who took office a week ago, was no exception. After a meeting with his counterpart in Chișinău, the pro-Western Vasile Tofan, Niculescu stated that the Republic of Moldova and Romania would accelerate the completion of joint infrastructure and energy projects and strengthen their economic ties. He added that Romania reaffirms its support for the Republic of Moldova regarding its European integration process, security, and the consolidation of its energy independence. Bucharest also advocates for the opening of the final two negotiating clusters for the Republic of Moldova’s accession to the European Union by the end of this year, and has pledged technical assistance to help align national legislation with EU law. In turn, the Moldovan Prime Minister Tofan stated that his team aims to accelerate joint projects with Romania, particularly those focused on connectivity between the two states. Priorities include the construction of several bridges across the Prut, the river that forms the border, as well as the modernization of roads and the streamlining of border crossing points. The two officials discussed accelerating electrical interconnection projects, as well as the possibility that, starting with the next cold season, the Republic of Moldova could receive natural gas from the Neptun Deep field in the Black Sea. Vasile Tofan also noted that the Republic of Moldova seeks to attract more Romanian investment in sectors such as industry, energy, technology, and infrastructure, and also to create opportunities for participation in the future reconstruction of neighboring Ukraine, which has been invaded by Russian forces. The Prime Minister Luca Niculescu began his visit with meetings with representatives of the Embassy and the Consulate General of Romania in Chișinău. He also held a meeting with the Metropolitan of Bessarabia, Antonie, who is canonically subordinate to the Orthodox Patriarchate in Bucharest. The Prime Minister further met with representatives of Romanian companies carrying out investment projects in the Republic of Moldova; he welcomed the fact that these companies have created approximately 12,000 jobs in the neighboring state, and noted that bilateral trade reached about 4.5 billion Euros last year.
